subject: physics
note: Figure-free parts only. Q7(c) (ray diagram) and Q2–6, Q8, Q10 left out: they need a figure or a drawing

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The second, metre and kilogram are all SI units of base quantities. Name two other base quantities whose SI units are not stated above.
parts.scheme: any two of: electric current, temperature, amount of substance [1] each

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Circle the value for the prefix deci.   10⁻⁹   10⁻⁶   10⁻³   10⁻²   10⁻¹   10³   10⁶   10⁹   10¹²

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Rearrange the following prefixes in order from the largest value to the smallest value.   n   μ   G   m   k
parts.scheme: G, k, m, μ, n [1]

questions.stem: A small object is placed in front of a thin converging lens.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define the focal length of a converging lens.
parts.scheme: distance between the optical centre and the focal point [1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Describe briefly an experiment to determine the focal length of such a lens.
parts.scheme: distant object focused on a screen [1]; adjust until the image is sharp, lens-to-screen distance = f [1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Other than the location and the magnification of the image, state two other characteristics of the image formed.
parts.scheme: virtual [1]; upright [1]

questions.stem:
The owner of a house records the details of the electricity usage for one day (Fig. 9.1).
appliance — power rating / W — time switched on / hours — energy used / kWh
TV and computer — 1000 — 2.0 — ....
kettle — 2000 — 0.20 — ....
lights — 800 — 3.0 — ....
water heater — 3500 — 0.20 — ....
air conditioner — 1500 — 6.0 — ....

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Complete Fig. 9.1 by calculating the amount of energy used by each appliance.
parts.scheme: 2.0, 0.40, 2.4, 0.70, 9.0 kWh — 1 mark for all correct values

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The cost of electricity is 31 cents per unit. Calculate the cost of the electricity usage for one day.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The wires supplying electric current to the water heater are thicker than those supplying current to the lights. Explain why this is necessary.
parts.scheme: higher power → higher current; thick wire → lower resistance; reduces energy/power loss or prevents overheating — 2 marks for 3 points, 1 mark for 1–2 points

questions.stem:
A company makes insulating bowls to keep food cool. Bowls made of polystyrene and of paper cardboard are filled with 200 g of ice at 0 °C. The mass of water (melted ice) is recorded every 5 minutes (Table 11.1).
time / min: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
polystyrene, without lid / g: 0, 2, 9, 13, 20, 30
polystyrene, with lid / g: 0, 0, 5, 9, 14, 23
paper cardboard, without lid / g: 0, 12, 25, 44, 58, 79
paper cardboard, with lid / g: 0, 5, 14, 30, 45, 63

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State one other variable that should be kept constant to ensure a fair test.
parts.scheme: e.g. size of bowl / size of ice cubes / surrounding temperature [1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Using the information from Table 11.1, suggest which material is better for insulation and explain your choice.
parts.scheme: polystyrene, with data from the table [1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Using ideas about thermal processes, suggest one reason for the difference in the mass of water collected with and without lid for both materials.
parts.scheme: lid traps air, a poor conductor / less conduction; OR less radiation reaches the ice [1]; reject convection or evaporation; if more than one process is stated, mark only the first

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: State and explain whether the bowl should be light-coloured or dark-coloured.
parts.scheme: light-coloured; poorer absorber of (infra-red) radiation [1]; reject "absorber of heat"

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: An ice maker takes in water at 25.0 °C and gives out ice cubes at −3.0 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J/(g °C); specific latent heat of fusion of water = 340 J/g; specific heat capacity of ice = 2.1 J/(g °C).

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by specific latent heat of fusion of water is 340 J / g.
parts.scheme: 340 J / energy / per 1 g / change between solid and liquid / at constant temperature: all points 2 m, 2–4 points 1 m; zero if a change in temperature is suggested

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why the internal energy of water decreases even though the temperature of water remains constant as it solidifies into ice.
parts.scheme: potential energy of the particles decreases (distance decreases / attraction increases) while kinetic energy is unchanged [1]

parts.label: (e)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the total amount of energy transferred as 500 g of water at 25.0 °C is cooled to form ice at −3.0 °C.
parts.scheme: Q = mcΔθ = 52 500 J; Q = ml = 170 000 J; Q = mcΔθ = 3 150 J; total 226 000 J (or 230 000 J) — [1] for each of the 2 formulae, [1] for the final answer

questions.stem: A doctor uses a radioactive isotope, iodine-131, to determine the volume of blood in a patient's body. Iodine-131 decays by emitting beta particles and gamma rays.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State two differences between beta particles and gamma rays.
parts.scheme: any 2: electron vs EM wave; more ionising; less penetrating; charged vs uncharged; mass vs no mass

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Some iodine-131 is injected and spreads evenly through the blood after twelve minutes. Nine samples of blood, each 2.0 cm³, are taken at two-minute intervals (Fig. 12.1, background subtracted).
sample number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
time after injection / min: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18
count rate / per second: 0, 4, 12, 18, 28, 40, 38, 36, 40

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the reason why the count rates of samples 6 to 9 are not constant throughout.
parts.scheme: nuclear decay is random and spontaneous [1]

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: The average value of the last four samples is the average count rate from 2.0 cm³ of blood. Determine the volume of blood in the patient's body which has a total count rate of 144 000 per second.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Iodine-131 (I) has nucleon number 131 and atomic number 53. It decays into Xenon (Xe) by emitting beta radiation. Write the nuclear decay equation.
parts.scheme: ¹³¹₅₃I → ¹³¹₅₄Xe + ⁰₋₁β [1]

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Sample number 9 is kept. The count rate is measured after 16 days. Estimate the count rate given that the half-life of iodine-131 is 8.0 days.
parts.scheme: 2 half-lives [1]; 40 / 2² = 10 counts per second [1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: State two factors the doctor must consider when selecting the radioactive isotope to be used for this purpose.
parts.scheme: short half-life [1]; not poisonous to the body [1]; do not accept "harmful" (too general) or "able to penetrate the skin"
